one-site.title: A rule placed at one site
one-site.lookFor:
- Name what the rule protects, such as a field, a kind of input or an effect, and search for that, rather than for the kind of code that holds the rule.
- Send the input the rule now catches in by every other route, and see whether it gets past:
  - the operation's other entry points, such as a `stream()` beside a `complete()`;
  - routes that replace the value after the rule has run, such as raw overrides and hooks;
  - other implementations of the same rule, including a helper the codebase already has;
  - other handlers and readers of the same data, in this repository and in any consumer you were given.

  A route where it gets past is a finding. So are two implementations that disagree: say what each does.
- For a validation rule, find every read of the validated input, including reads by presence, by truthiness, or by an exact match whose `else` lets everything else through. A read that skips the validation is a finding.
- For a new way to stop, fail or skip at a boundary, follow each path that can carry on past it, such as finish hooks, input that arrives while they run, and workers whose lifetime nothing joins. A path that carries on is a finding.
- For a rule about identity, such as which request, job or record a selector means, find every place that resolves or retires by that identity. A place that matches on only part of it is a finding.
- For a field added to a stored type, find every place a sibling field is spelled out, such as codecs, serializers, projections and views. A place that drops the new field is a finding.
- For a rule about who may see or do something, such as a channel filter, a mute or a credential grant, follow every way content leaves: results, excerpts, errors and logs. A way out that skips the rule is a finding.
- Read the lines around the change, and any code or comment that says it follows the changed function. Another instance of the class the change says it fixes, or a follower that no longer matches, is a finding.
one-site.name: reference:code-review/rule-placed-at-one-site

pieces.title: Each piece and the test aimed at it
pieces.name: reference:code-review/each-piece-and-its-test

vs-base.title: Comparison with main
vs-base.lookFor:
- Take inputs around the shapes the change touches, and their neighbours, and work out what main's code and the change's code each do with them, at the boundary callers see: what the next component does with the output, and what the program finally sends. Include values the old code ignored and the new code may refuse, and sequences where earlier state matters, such as a history that a later message changes. A difference the change doesn't seem to intend, or one its changelog and text don't name, is a finding.
- Feed each entry point bad input too, and compare what an operator reads from each side, such as a clean error on main and a stack trace on the change. A difference the change doesn't name is a finding.
- For a new module or option that is on by default: what does the program send with it on, and with it off? A difference that nothing names is a finding.
- For a change that consolidates or replaces an existing path: list what the old path answered for each kind of input it handled. An input the new path answers differently, such as an error the new code classifies more narrowly, is a finding.
vs-base.name: reference:code-review/comparison-with-main

await.title: A check and its effect, with a gap between them
await.lookFor:
- Find each place where the code checks a condition, such as a policy, a stop flag, an idle state or a cached value, and other work can run before the effect the check guards. The gap is usually an await. It can also be a lock released or not yet taken, another process or connection writing the same store, or another component that commits the effect.
- Picture the condition changing inside that gap: a stop arriving, a second request, another writer committing, the room or record going away. Does the effect still happen on the old answer? Is the guard checked again inside the step that commits the effect? Is a value read before the gap, such as an owner, a set or a key, carried into the effect? A guard that can be stale when its effect commits is a finding. Give the interleaving that breaks it.
await.name: reference:code-review/await-between-check-and-effect

replay.title: An operation that can run again or stop partway
replay.lookFor:
- For an operation that a request key, a retry or a replay can run again: replay it after each outcome the first run can have, a commit, a no-op, a refusal and a failure. A replay returns what the first run returned and does nothing more. A replay that acts again, aborts work that followed it, or returns something else is a finding.
- Check each fallback path's result as carefully as the first path's. A fallback that returns or records the wrong outcome is a finding.
- For an operation with several steps, one of which can't be undone: let each later step fail in turn. An irreversible step that runs before a step that can still fail is a finding, and so is a failure that can't resume in place.
replay.name: reference:code-review/run-again-or-stop-partway

drops.title: A branch that drops, refuses, skips or falls back
drops.lookFor:
- Find each branch that drops, refuses, skips, defaults or falls back. Look for them at each `catch`, early `return`, `?? default`, refusal, and retry that gives up.
- Picture it firing in production. Can whoever runs the code tell it from success? The caller can learn it from a typed error or a field in the result, the operator from a log line or a count that names what was dropped and why, and an agent from a notice in a place a live agent reads. A branch that fires with nothing to show for it is a finding. Where silence is the contract, as for a filter doing its job, it isn't.
- Ask the same of each thing the change can cause to be dropped further along, such as a tool, a marker or a field.
- Read the trace itself. One written to a stdout that a protocol or another command reads, or one that logs a raw value rather than a name, a size or a hash, is a finding.
- Find what runs failed work again, and how often. Failed work that reruns on every check, with nothing to stop it, is a finding.
drops.name: reference:code-review/drops-and-fallbacks

every-event.title: Something written, kept or done on every event
every-event.lookFor:
- For each write or retained value that happens on every event, such as a receipt, a journal record, a checkpoint, a request preimage, a state file rewritten on each update, or an in-memory map that lives as long as its store: picture a resident running for weeks. Does each write stay constant in size, or grow with the history behind it? Growth with no bound, such as no cap, rotation, expiry or reclaim, is a finding.
- For work added to every call: what does it cost a caller who never uses the feature? A cost that grows with history, or one that every caller pays for a feature few use, is a finding.
every-event.name: reference:code-review/every-event

runtime.title: Code that depends on its runtime, or evidence others will cite
runtime.lookFor:
- For code that uses sockets, timers, the wall clock, process and error events, child processes, file paths or the test runner's own APIs: would it behave the same on every runtime the code will meet? For a package others install, that's the range it declares (`engines`, or `requires-python`), from its floor to the latest release, and a runtime one consumer pins is one point inside it. For code that only its own deployment runs, it's the runtime installed there. Behaviour that depends on the runtime is a finding, and so is such behaviour tested at only one end of the range. Remember that the wall clock can step back, after an NTP step or a VM restore.
- For a platform the project's own tests don't run on, such as Windows when they run on Linux: does the code, or its test, rest on an assumption about the platform rather than on the runtime's own source for that behaviour? A test that encodes the same assumption as the code it tests is a finding.
- For evidence the change publishes about another component, such as a conformance run or a reproduction: which revision of that component, and which runtime, did it run on? Evidence from a stale revision or the wrong runtime, or evidence with no label, is a finding.
runtime.name: reference:code-review/runtime-and-evidence

states.title: The states the code tells apart
states.lookFor:
- List the states this code must tell apart: first run or later, empty or not, restarted or not, never had or had and lost, present and intact or present and damaged, and any others its data can be in.
- Send each state through the code, and see which branch it takes. Two states that share a branch they shouldn't are a finding. A common case is an existence check standing in for "never had", so that something which was there and has gone takes the path for something that never was.
- Check each test and each claim in the change's text against each state. A test or claim that holds only in the state its author pictured, such as one that holds only once a counter is above zero, or only before a restart, is a finding.
states.name: reference:code-review/states-the-code-tells-apart

callers.title: What callers will notice
callers.name: reference:code-review/what-callers-notice

meaning.title: A value and what its readers take it to mean
meaning.name: reference:code-review/value-and-its-meaning

reliance.title: What the code relies on another component to do
reliance.lookFor:
- Find each place where the code, a comment or the change's text relies on how another component behaves: another module in this repository, a dependency, a consumer, a spec, or the runtime.
- Read that component's own code or text, at the version the change will run with, rather than from memory or from a comment that describes it.
- Check what it actually does at that point: what it selects, returns, retries, throws or respawns, and in what order it decides. A reliance the component's code contradicts is a finding. Give the component's place as one of its places.
reliance.name: reference:code-review/reliance-on-another-component

waits.title: What a test waits for, and what its verdict means
waits.lookFor:
- For each wait in a test, such as a sleep, a timer, a polling loop or a fixed delay before an assertion: picture the machine under load. Does the test wait for the event that completes the phase the next step depends on, such as a record of the request a fake received or a completion flag, with time only as an outer bound? A fixed delay standing in for that event is a finding, since load uses it up.
- For each time bound a test asserts, where the suite may run under a CPU quota: is it judged by one wall-clock maximum? CPU time, or a mean or percentile of lag chosen by the property, holds up under a quota, and one wall-clock maximum is a finding.
- For each test whose verdict is that something didn't happen: does it also assert that it reached the point where it could have happened, such as the held call being entered or the state it races on existing? A test that would pass by never getting there is a finding of kind "test".
- For each fake or mock of another component: does it behave the way that component's source does where the test's verdict depends on it, such as wrapping a failure the same way, or retrying the same number of times? A fake that differs there is a finding.
waits.name: reference:code-review/what-a-test-verdict-means

text.title: The text against the code
text.lookFor:
- Check each claim in the text against the code at the head: what it says the code does, what it says was tested, the numbers it states, and the names it uses. Look hardest at the words that widen a claim, such as "every", "only", "never", "all" and "not even". A claim the code contradicts, or that nothing in the code or tests supports, is a finding of kind "text" when it would mislead someone who acts on it, such as a caller, an operator, a maintainer or an agent, in a case that happens, however rarely. Advice is checked on the path where it's given, since that's when someone follows it. Quote the claim, and say who it would mislead and how.
- Text needs to be true for its reader, not complete. A claim that leaves a case out without saying anything false about it, or that is wider than the code only in a case nobody meets, isn't a finding, and neither is wording you would only improve.
- A claim about several things: check each one, since a grep count or one combined run stops at what it can see.
- Text elsewhere about what the change alters or corrects: for each behaviour the change alters, and each description the change corrects, find the comments, docstrings, docs and test headers elsewhere that describe the same thing (grep the names involved), and check each at the head. One the change made false, or one still saying what the change corrected, is a finding of kind "text", though the diff doesn't touch it.
- An example in the text: would it run as its reader would copy it, including with a value past the API's defaults? A string that gives advice: does the advice work when followed? An example or advice that fails is a finding.
- A claim about why the code is as it is: does the commit that introduced it, and what it depended on at that date, bear it out?
- A test named as evidence: does the test do what its name says? A test's name isn't evidence of what it ran.
- A promise of further work, in the text or a reply: is that work still needed?
- The description's rent pass, such as a "What each part is for" section, is the one text that has to be complete: it's where the author weighs each part the change adds, so a part it leaves out goes unweighed. For each part the diff adds or changes, such as a function, a field, a check, a rule or a test helper, find where the pass weighs it, by what it buys or what fails without it. A part it doesn't weigh is a finding of kind "text": name the part and where the diff adds it. When this review follows an earlier one, the diff is this round's, so its parts are the ones to look for, whatever the pass says about earlier rounds.
text.name: reference:code-review/text-against-the-code

stored.title: Stored data across versions and crashes
stored.lookFor:
- Find every write the change adds or alters to anything that outlives the process and is read back as state: a Chronicle record kind or payload, a state slot, a blob, a JSON file beside a store, a pref or setting. Logs, and caches rebuilt from other data, are outside this lens. For each, compare the head's writer with the base's; the scratch holds both. A field added, removed, renamed or given a new meaning is a change of shape. A change of shape is a finding when nothing handles what is already stored: no version beside the data, no migration, and no reader that accepts the older shape (the next point checks the readers).
- For each reader of stored data, list the shapes it can meet: what the base's writer left, what the head's writer leaves, a write cut off partway, and a file or record that is missing. Send each shape through the reader. A reader that throws on an older shape, misreads it, or quietly fills a default (a missing field read as 0, false or empty) where that default changes what the record means, is a finding. So is a shape the head writes that the base's reader would misread after a rollback, unless the change says a rollback isn't supported.
- For each migration, check what marks it done, and when. A marker written before the work it vouches for has succeeded, or never written at all, is a finding. Stop the migration after each step in turn, as a crash would, and start it again. A step that can't resume, or that repeats work or loses data on the second run, is a finding. So is a migration that changes data in place with no copy to go back to.
- For each write that replaces such state, check that a write cut off midway can't leave a file or record that later reads take as whole. A file written in place rather than written beside it and renamed, a rename with no sync of the file and its directory, or an "already there" check that a damaged copy passes, is a finding.
- Check the tests. Does any test give the head's reader data in the shape the base, or an older release, wrote? A change of shape whose tests only read what the head itself just wrote is a finding.
- Find every SQLite connection the change opens or configures, and read what it sets for `journal_mode`, `synchronous` and the busy timeout against what the project states for them: in its AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING or other docs, or in comments where its other connections are opened, which search finds. SQLite's own default for `synchronous` is FULL unless it was built otherwise, even under WAL, and SQLite waits 0 for a busy database unless a timeout is set: a fresh `bun:sqlite` connection leaves that as it is, and Python's `sqlite3.connect` sets 5 s unless given another `timeout`. A connection whose settings go against what the project states, or that leaves to a default a value the project states, is a finding.
stored.name: reference:code-review/stored-data-across-versions

errors.title: What an error tells its reader
errors.lookFor:
- Find each error text the diff adds or changes: a thrown error's message, a tool result marked as an error, a refusal, a notice or marker put into an agent's context, and a reason string that a caller puts into a larger sentence, and each status or health line, warning or notice a UI shows.
- **Find its reader first.** Follow where the text goes. It may reach an agent, as a tool result or a notice in its context. It may go to the caller of a library, which wraps it, logs it or passes it on. Or it may reach only an operator's log. Or a person may read it in a UI. Judge the rest of these checks for that reader.
  - **Text an agent reads** that names something only an operator can change, such as an environment variable, a configuration field or a log file the agent can't open, is a finding.
  - **In a library,** a thrown message's reader is the library's caller, so judge it for them.
  - **Where a layer quotes host-facing text to an agent,** such as a library's message passed through as a notice's reason, the finding belongs at the layer that quotes it.
  - **Where the route leaves the code you were given,** say you couldn't follow it rather than guess.
- **A marker in an agent's context:** text that stands in for content left out of it, such as an image or a tool result. The agent re-reads it every turn, and it sits in cached prefixes. Does it say what happened, and whether the content can still be reached, in as few words as carry that? Any reason it gives must hold on every path that writes it. The checks for failures below don't apply to a routine omission.
- **A state shown to a person,** such as a status or health line, a warning or a notice in a UI: would the person seeing it know what happened, what it means for what they look after (whether it's affected now, and whether the state will pass on its own or needs them), and what to do, or that there's nothing to do? A line in a library's terms is a finding. So is one that leaves out, or cuts to its column's width, what they'd act on, and an all-clear such as "healthy" shown when the code couldn't look.
- **What happened, first.** Does it lead with the outcome, in the reader's own terms? Those are the tool and argument names the reader used, and the value it sent where that shows the mistake. Class names, spec sections, protocol codes and internal field names in text an agent reads are a finding, since they belong in the operator's log.
- **Whether anything changed.** For a call that changes things, does it say that nothing was done, what was done, or that the outcome is unknown?
  - "Nothing was done" where the failure can come partway is a finding. An example is a loop that writes one item at a time.
  - So is a success message sent before the effect is confirmed.
- **What the reader can do.** Does it name a remedy the reader has: a tool they can call, an argument they can pass, or a wait with its length? Where the reader named something that doesn't exist and the code knows what does, does it give the candidates or the closest one? Follow each remedy through the code from where the message is given. A remedy that can't work there is a finding:
  - a larger limit, past the deployment's ceiling;
  - an edit to a file the code doesn't read;
  - a route or command the reader has no tool for;
  - a retry of a refusal that will repeat.

  Where nothing the reader does will help, does it say so plainly, say that calling again won't change it, and name who can, such as whoever runs the host?
- **It reads as a failure.** A failure returned as an ordinary result, without the error flag its protocol has (such as `isError`), is a finding. So is a normal outcome reported as an error.
- **It reads once when composed.** Where another layer puts the text into a larger sentence, read the whole as its reader gets it. Each of these is a finding:
  - a doubled prefix (`Error: Error: …`, `RPC error -32602: RPC error -32602: …`);
  - a full sentence dropped where a clause belongs;
  - a remedy that contradicts the frame's.
- **Code that matches it.** This is the message-text case of what callers notice. Before a message changes, search the repository, its tests and any consumers you were given for code that matches on its text: `startsWith`, `includes`, `===`, a regular expression, or a test assertion on the string. Rewording text that code matches, without first moving the match to a code or a typed field, is a finding.
- **File each finding once.** When a finding about an error's text would also fit another lens you were given, file it once, under this lens.
errors.name: reference:code-review/what-an-error-tells-its-reader
